target.thesis: Gubelmann's Kantian criterion has no principled stopping point at the skin without biological chauvinism. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines, it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting whole, so 'LLMs cannot speak' reduces to 'parts as such do not speak'. The whole may be a speaker, with authorship layered across levels and fixed by a separate attribution rule. A distinct third kind of author is not established.
target.headline: Gubelmann's Kantian criterion of organismhood, on which parts are reciprocally means and ends and the whole organises and maintains itself, does not fix a level of attribution. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting system. This turns 'LLMs cannot speak' into the trivial claim that organs do not speak, and it yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy.
target.target: Gubelmann's organismic ground. It also targets proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora), which assume the author must be an individual human.
target.sketch: For Kant a natural purpose is a whole whose parts exist for and through one another. Nothing in that definition privileges the skin-bounded individual. Firms, newsrooms and customer-service operations are self-organising and self-maintaining through hiring, repair and revenue. Within them, deployed LLMs are retrained, patched and rewarded according to the whole's goals, and their outputs figure in the whole's reproduction of its own conditions. If goals set by such a whole count as autonomously set, which Gubelmann's cognitive-autonomy concession for LLMs invites, then speech acts through LLMs are performed by the whole and by no part. This differs from the proxy view, because no single human principal is the author and no individual's intention is being relayed. It also differs from Gubelmann's denial, because the speech act is genuine and the whole has the intentions. The premise the argument turns on is that his three-way separation of material, cognitive and moral autonomy can be satisfied at the level of an assemblage. He cannot rule that out without an independent principle of individuation, and Kant supplies none. His reply that only biological individuals qualify would restore the biological chauvinism he elsewhere disclaims.

findings.part: Target claim: proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora) assume the author must be an individual human
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now)", Philosophy & Technology, 2024 (on Green & Michel); Sneddon/other, "Why Proxy Accounts of AI Speech Acts Fail", American Philosophical Quarterly, 2026
findings.what_they_say: Gubelmann reads Green and Michel's proxy speech as covering cases like a city-council representative who speaks only in that representative role. The APQ abstract describes the proxy account as making the chatbot a stand-in for a human speaker or a corporation. Nickel, as reported in the Inquiry paper, locates responsibility with persons or companies, or with nobody.
findings.note: Proxy accounts already allow organisational principals, so the thesis cannot say they require an individual human; it can only say the whole remains a principal for whom the LLM stands in, not a whole of which the LLM is an organ.

findings.source: Arora, "Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions", Philosophy & Technology, 2024; characterised in "Who asserts when no one asserts?", Synthese, 2026
findings.what_they_say: Arora holds that some machine utterances are proxy assertions made on behalf of the designers and/or deployers. The 2026 Synthese paper reports that Arora insists genuine assertion needs a conscious principal who can be held accountable.
findings.note: The principal can be plural ('designers and/or deployers'), so the individual-human attribution holds only if 'conscious, accountable principal' is read as an individual; I did not read Arora's full text.

findings.part: Motivation: no single human principal is the author
findings.source: Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion, Inquiry, 2024 (arXiv 2410.16645)
findings.what_they_say: They argue proxy-assertion has a potentially fatal problem: typical proxy cases have a clear principal, but in typical LLM-chatbot interactions there is no clear candidate for the principal. They also note Arora's account classifies talking clocks and thermometers as proxy asserters.
findings.note: This is the premise the thesis uses against proxy views, already published, so it works as evidence rather than as a rival.

findings.source: "Why Proxy Accounts of AI Speech Acts Fail", American Philosophical Quarterly 63(3), 2026
findings.what_they_say: The abstract argues the proxy account neglects the relational nature of speech, so no human can be held responsible for most of what a chatbot says. Only the abstract was visible.
findings.note: Independent critique of proxy views on responsibility grounds; it does not propose the whole-as-speaker alternative, as far as the abstract shows.

findings.part: Whole as speaker; authorship layered across levels; separate attribution rule
findings.source: Schmidt, "Can Artificial Agents be Authors?", Philosophy & Technology 38, 2025
findings.what_they_say: Schmidt defines institutional authorship using Searle's speech act theory and concludes that artificial agents cannot be authors. He considers collective authorship as an explanation of generative-AI output and says it would still not make the artificial agent an author. He notes Meijers's view that collective speech acts are sui generis.
findings.note: Closest philosophical treatment of collective authorship for AI output; it lacks the Kantian organ/whole mechanism and Gubelmann's autonomy trichotomy, but a referee will raise it.

findings.part: The whole (firm or assemblage) as the agent that sets goals
findings.source: List, "Group Agency and Artificial Intelligence", Philosophy & Technology, 2021 (reference list cites List & Pettit 2011)
findings.what_they_say: The paper treats group agents as special cases of AI systems whose hardware is social, not electronic. It develops a parallel between group agency and AI agency, including responsibility.
findings.note: Group-agent theory already supplies the idea that a whole can be an agent without being an individual human, but through the List–Pettit route and not through Kantian natural purposes. I read only an excerpt.

findings.part: Kant's definition gives no skin-bounded privilege
findings.source: "The 'Whole' Truth about Biological Individuality in Kant's Account of Living Nature", Kantian Review, 2023
findings.what_they_say: The paper argues that the reciprocal causality between a self-organizing whole and its parts, which Kant takes to characterize a natural end, is not limited to organisms. It says self-organizing wholes at various biological levels may count as individuals, depending on how far reflective judgement represents their parts as a natural end.
findings.note: Kantian-scholarly support for the premise that the definition does not stop at the organism, but it concerns biological levels, not firms, and it stresses the regulative status of the concept.

findings.part: Dilemma: stop at the skin, or be a biological chauvinist
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now)", Philosophy & Technology, 2024; Kantian Review 2023 on extrinsic ends
findings.what_they_say: Gubelmann's stated line is organism versus engineered mechanism: LLMs are artifacts, mechanisms with no autonomy or intrinsic goals. He also envisages 'non-human, but equally non-artificial agents'. The Kantian Review paper reports Kant distinguishing natural ends from extrinsic ends designed by a rational agent for an external purpose.
findings.note: His stopping point looks like artifactuality, not the skin or biology. Whether a firm counts as non-artificial is a live question, so the thesis needs an argument that a self-maintaining firm is not an extrinsic end, and not only a charge of chauvinism.

findings.part: Gubelmann's autonomy concession and the three-way separation
findings.source: Gubelmann, 2024, Springer HTML; Do Large Language Models Defend Inferentialist Semantics?, ResearchGate preprint
findings.what_they_say: Gubelmann describes mechanisms as materially, cognitively and morally heteronomous. He says single-cell organisms are materially autonomous: they maintain a membrane and metabolise. He also says LLMs have no material autonomy and do not care about continued existence. A secondary source says LLMs 'exhibit Kantian cognitive autonomy, see Gubelmann (2024)'.
findings.note: The text supports the three-way structure the thesis uses. The 'cognitive-autonomy concession' appears in my results only through a secondary paraphrase, and Gubelmann himself ties intentions to autonomous goal-setting. Check the original wording. His membrane example also leans on the skin-boundary image the thesis attacks.

findings.part: Organisations as self-producing wholes whose communications belong to the system, not to its members
findings.source: Luhmann on autopoietic social systems, via ScienceDirect topic overview; "Luhmann's theory of autopoietic social systems"
findings.what_they_say: Luhmann holds that social systems are self-organizing and self-reproducing and consist of communications, not individuals. Organisations reproduce themselves through decisions. Action is still needed to ascribe communications to actors.
findings.note: This is the empirical and sociological anticipation of 'the whole communicates, attribution is a separate step', and it was not framed as an answer to LLM speakerhood or to Gubelmann.

findings.part: Layered authorship that no single component holds
findings.source: "The role of generative AI in academic and scientific authorship: an autopoietic perspective", AI & Society, 2024
findings.what_they_say: Applying Luhmann's social systems theory, the paper concludes that the autopoietic nature of authorship cannot be reduced to any one component in the structural coupling of author, scientific system and technology.
findings.note: It already applies the autopoietic whole to GenAI authorship, but with author and technology as distinct coupled systems. It does not say the LLM is an organ of a goal-setting whole, and it has no speech-act or Kantian criterion.

findings.part: LLM speech acts as extensions of human collective intentionality
findings.source: "Communicative Action in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Theorizing LLMs as Communicative and Strategic Agents", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The paper treats LLMs as quasi-social agents whose functional speech acts extend human collective intentionality. It says constitutive authority stays with human agents who have genuine intentionality, and it cites Gubelmann.
findings.note: It places LLM speech inside collective intentionality and keeps authority with humans, which is a rival on where the intentions sit; it says LLMs cannot perform genuine illocutionary acts.

findings.part: Most recent syntheses of proxy and functionalist views
findings.source: "Who asserts when no one asserts? Functionalism, proxy responsibility, and conversational ideals in the age of LLMs", Synthese, 2026; "Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The Synthese paper contrasts functionalist accounts with proxy views that trace accountability to the humans or organizations behind the system. The P&T paper says proxy, proto-assertion and AI-testimony accounts typically keep the idea that assertion requires an asserter, and then proposes a different route.
findings.note: These are where the current map of positions sits. Neither obviously contains a whole-as-speaker position, but I saw only abstracts and excerpts.

findings.part: A separate attribution rule that fixes authorship
findings.source: "Fluid Agency in AI Systems: A Case for Functional...", arXiv 2601.02633 (legal analysis)
findings.what_they_say: The paper notes that UK copyright law gives computer-generated works to the person who made the arrangements necessary for creation, a pragmatic construct to fill an attribution gap. It also says employers are generally first owners of employees' works.
findings.note: Existing legal practice has a rule separating attribution from who or what produced the text, which the thesis can cite as precedent for its 'separate attribution rule'.

findings.part: Empirical basis: maintained human–LLM pipelines behave as wholes
findings.source: "Human–AI collectives most accurately diagnose clinical vignettes" (PMC); "Collective Cognition in Hybrid Groups: A Network Science Synthesis", arXiv 2607.05593; Barandiaran & Pérez-Verdugo, "Generative midtended cognition", Synthese, 2025
findings.what_they_say: Hybrid human–AI collectives outperform human-only and LLM-only ones in diagnosis. The network-science synthesis reports group-level properties that are not inherited from individual agents. Barandiaran and Pérez-Verdugo extend enactivist autonomy to sociotechnical wholes.
findings.note: These show group-level organisation, and in the enactivist case group-level autonomy, but none concerns authorship or speech acts.

finding.what_is_left: Gubelmann's organism/mechanism criterion, applied to a maintained human–LLM pipeline, does not by itself exclude the pipeline's firm or newsroom, because his own stopping point is artifactuality and not biology. If such a whole counts as self-maintaining and self-goal-setting, an LLM's outputs are speech acts of the whole and not of the LLM as a part. This differs from proxy accounts, which already allow corporate principals but treat the LLM as a stand-in, because here the LLM is an organ of the whole and no one's intention is relayed. Group-agent theory, Luhmannian autopoiesis and collective-authorship work have already made the general moves that a whole can be the author and that attribution is a separate step. What remains for the thesis is the specific Kantian argument that Gubelmann's three autonomies can be met at the level of an assemblage, together with the claim that this reduces 'LLMs cannot speak' to 'parts as such do not speak'. It also has to show why a firm is not just another extrinsic end, in Kant's sense of a thing designed by a rational agent for an external purpose.
finding.not_found: I found no source that applies Kant's natural-purpose criterion to firms or human–LLM pipelines to argue that a whole speaks through its LLM organs. I found no published reply to Gubelmann that argues the organism criterion should stop at the assemblage, and no text that uses the proxy view as a foil in exactly this way. I did not find Kant's own remarks on whether non-organic wholes such as states can be natural purposes; I did not search for that, and a referee will likely raise it. I also did not retrieve Gubelmann's explicit disclaimer of biological chauvinism or the exact wording of his cognitive-autonomy concession for LLMs, so those two premises are unchecked against his text. Most of the philosophy sources were seen as abstracts or excerpts. Psychology and cognitive-science work on how people attribute speakerhood or authorship to human–AI wholes (as opposed to collective-performance studies) was not searched. Paywalled work, German-language Luhmann-and-AI literature, and the legal and organisational-theory literature on corporate speech were largely invisible to me, so the absence of hits is weak evidence.

sep.why: The theses argue that a human–LLM organisation can be a collective speaker and author of speech acts, which engages collective intentionality, Kantian organismic or natural-purpose accounts of whole–part goal-directedness (teleology in biology), and the theory of speech acts.

findings.position: A whole made of members can be the subject of intentional states once it has an internal structure with roles and decision mechanisms. Its members then function as parts or positions within it.
findings.who: Tuomela (we-groups as organized institutional entities); French; Hindriks's status account; Pettit and List (group agents)
findings.quote: a we-mode group […] is a collective artefact and indeed an organized institutional entity […]. Group members are viewed as functioning in group positions
findings.note: The move from parts as such not speaking to the structured whole as subject is the standard subject-account move; the human–LLM pipeline is only a new kind of part.

findings.position: Subjecthood is conferred or fixed by a separate ascription or attribution criterion. This is interpretationism, plus conditions on rational unity that justify the ascription.
findings.who: Tollefsen (intentional stance applied to groups; rational unity); Rovane; Hindriks (status account)
findings.quote: making groups' status as intentional subjects dependent on whether their behavior can be interpreted as intentional
findings.note: This resembles the thesis's 'separate attribution rule'; the entry also warns that mere interpretability is not enough and that internal structure must justify the ascription.

findings.position: Intentions are layered. Individual intentions can be derivative from a higher-level joint intention, for example moving a pawn derives from playing chess.
findings.who: Sellars (we-derivative vs primary I-referential intentions)
findings.quote: My intention to move a pawn on the chessboard is derivative from our intention to play a game of chess.
findings.note: This is a nearby model of part-level attitudes fixed by whole-level ones. It concerns intentions, not authorship.

findings.position: Group attitudes may be discontinuous with member attitudes, and the group can be an agent at its own level. This allows authorship to sit at the group level while members stay non-authors of the group's output.
findings.who: Pettit; List and Pettit
findings.quote: such groups fulfill them as collective units of agency whose attitudes may be discontinuous with the attitudes of their members
findings.note: Gives the thesis a ready framework for a layered, whole-level speaker.

findings.position: The subject need not be a rational unity of agents. Two or more individuals can jointly form the subject, which is a lighter, non-organizational whole.
findings.who: Smith 2011; Rovane; Tollefsen; Pettit
findings.quote: two or more individuals jointly form the subject of their collective intentional attitudes
findings.note: Supports the idea that wholes can be subjects without a separate group mind.

findings.position: The Individual Ownership Thesis, with its naturalist and internalist versions, holds that intentionality belongs to individual minds or brains and cannot be fused into a super-subject. This resists 'the whole may be a speaker'.
findings.who: Most participants in the debate; Searle's internalism
findings.quote: Collective intentionality is had by the participating individuals, and all the intentionality an individual has is their own
findings.note: The thesis must say how the whole is a speaker without breaching ownership; the entry's answers are Tuomela's and Sellars's, where the whole is not an additional bearer.

findings.position: Attributions of intentionality to wholes are metaphorical shorthand. Even Tuomela says groups are agents only in a metaphorical sense.
findings.who: Quinton 1975; Tuomela 2007; Collingwood ('society is nothing over and above its members')
findings.quote: groups can but need not be taken as (singular) entities, and they are agents and persons only in a metaphorical sense
findings.note: A deflationary reading would make 'the whole may be a speaker' a façon de parler, so the thesis owes an argument against it.

findings.position: The naturalist version of the Individual Ownership Thesis ties intentionality to brains, and the entry rejects a 'Borg-like' integration of brains. Whether the skin is a principled boundary is an adjacent issue, though the entry does not call it biological chauvinism.
findings.who: Naturalist version of the Individual Ownership Thesis
findings.quote: any (primary) intentional state is a higher order feature of a brain. It is not the case that in collective intentionality, individual brains are integrated in a Borg-like manner
findings.note: A referee would push back that the skin boundary is motivated by ownership or autonomy, not chauvinism.

findings.position: Collective responsibility and agency require agency, intentionality or autonomy on the part of the bearer. Accounts of the whole's responsibility should not be discontinuous with accounts of its agency, which is relevant to who is the author or responsible party.
findings.who: Hindriks; Pettit 2007b; List and Pettit
findings.quote: there is no responsibility without agency, intentionality, freedom, or autonomy on the part of the entity to whom responsibility is ascribed
findings.note: Authorship and responsibility are likely to be tied together by a referee.

nearest_positions: Group-agent subject accounts requiring an organizational structure with roles and decision procedures — Pettit and List; Tuomela (we-groups as collective artefacts, members functioning in positions); French
Interpretationist or status-based attribution of intentionality to structured groups — Tollefsen; Rovane; Hindriks
Deflationary or individualist view that group agency is metaphorical and the Individual Ownership Thesis holds — Quinton; Tuomela's reductionist social ontology; Collingwood; Searle's internalism
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Gubelmann or any Kantian criterion of agency, LLMs or AI systems of any kind, human–machine pipelines, and speech or authorship as the target (as opposed to intention, belief or commitment). It does not discuss non-biological parts as organs of a goal-setting whole, nor 'biological chauvinism' as a charge against the skin boundary. It also has no discussion of whether layered authorship needs a third author-kind, so that conclusion gets no support or opposition from it.

findings.position: On Ginsborg's reading of Kant, self-regeneration and reproduction give organisms a natural purposiveness that artifacts lack. This is a principled boundary for the Kantian criterion, and it is not the skin or biological chauvinism. A maintained human–LLM pipeline would be an artifact-type whole and would not meet it.
findings.who: Hannah Ginsborg (2004), reading Kant and paralleling Aristotle
findings.quote: Kant thought that the regenerative and reproductive aspects of organisms lead us to attribute a kind of natural purposiveness that is absent in artifacts
findings.note: Undercuts the claim that the criterion has no principled stopping point. The thesis must argue that maintained pipelines meet the regenerative condition, or that the condition is itself chauvinist.

findings.position: Organizational accounts draw the whole's boundary by self-maintenance. A trait's function is its contribution to the organization that maintains the trait itself. This gives a non-skin, non-chauvinist criterion for what counts as a whole with parts.
findings.who: Schlosser 1998; McLaughlin 2001; Mossio, Saborido & Moreno 2009; Moreno & Mossio 2015
findings.quote: a trait token T has a function F when the performance of F by T contributes to the maintenance of the complex organization of the system, which in turn results in T's continued existence
findings.note: A pipeline maintained from outside, by humans, does not sustain its own parts. That is a candidate stopping point the thesis must address.

findings.position: Cummins-style functional analysis defines a part's function by its contribution to a larger system's capacity. It is explicitly not specific to biology and applies equally to artifacts. This is the move that makes the LLM an organ of a larger whole.
findings.who: Cummins 1975; Lewens 2004; extended to mechanisms by Craver 2007 and Maley & Piccinini 2017
findings.quote: there is nothing specifically biological about the pattern of explanation offered by functional analysis; it applies equally well, for example to the contributions made by the components of artifacts
findings.note: The entry offers a precedent for 'part of a whole' attributions that cross the organism/artifact line.

findings.position: The field-theoretic externalist account locates goal-directedness in an upper-level field that directs, without determining, the embedded parts. It claims full generality across living and non-living systems. It is criticized as too permissive to make sense of biological teleology.
findings.who: McShea 2012, 2016; Babcock & McShea 2021, 2024; critique by García-Valdecasas 2025
findings.quote: the goal-directed behavior of teleological systems arises because they are embedded in "upper-level fields" that direct but do not determine their activities
findings.note: A referee will use the permissiveness objection against a criterion that lets pipelines count as wholes with goals.

findings.position: For Kant, we inevitably understand organisms as teleological, but the teleology is a product of our cognitive faculties. This supports the thesis's idea that attribution is fixed by a separate rule, and it treats a Kantian purposiveness criterion as applying to whole systems taken as means and ends.
findings.who: Kant 1790; Zammito 2006; Lenoir 1982 on the teleo-mechanist strategy
findings.quote: the teleology we see in the natural world is only apparent; it is the product of our limited cognitive faculties
findings.note: Supports attribution being relative to an interpretive rule. It also raises the question of whether the Kantian criterion is observer-dependent.

findings.position: Derived and lifetime functions for traits that arise within a single organism's life, such as new concepts or antibodies, are grounded in differential persistence or retention. This gives a layered, non-evolutionary account of function that a maintained-pipeline view might draw on.
findings.who: Millikan 1984; Bouchard 2013; Garson 2017
findings.quote: using "differential persistence" and "differential retention" within an organism's lifespan to play the role that differential reproduction plays
findings.note: A possible resource for the layered-levels and maintenance claim.

nearest_positions: Kantian organism as both means and end, with natural purposiveness distinguishing organisms from artifacts — Kant, via Ginsborg (2004), Zammito, Lenoir
Organizational or self-maintenance accounts of function and of what counts as a whole — Moreno & Mossio, Schlosser, McLaughlin
Cummins-style causal-role functional analysis, which is domain-general, plus the McShea field account and its permissiveness critique — Cummins, Lewens, McShea, García-Valdecasas
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Everything about LLMs, speakers, authorship and attribution rules. The entry never mentions Gubelmann or any Kantian criterion applied to artificial language systems. It never addresses 'biological chauvinism' as an objection to a stopping point at the skin, or the idea of layered authorship across levels of a whole. It treats teleology and function only for biological and, in passing, artifact systems, not for linguistic agency.

findings.position: The entry defines speech acts through speaker meaning, so whether something counts as a speaker depends on intentional, overt commitment-undertaking. It does not depend on any species-based test. The thesis can build on this to ask which entity, part or whole, satisfies the condition.
findings.who: Green (the entry's author), drawing on Grice and Strawson
findings.quote: a speech act is a type of act that can be performed by speaker meaning that one is doing so
findings.note: gives a non-biological, agent-level criterion that the 'parts vs whole' move can use

findings.position: Speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment. This is a condition on an agent, not on a sentence or on any single component that produces words.
findings.who: Green 2013/2019, against Searle's 'recognition suffices'
findings.quote: speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment; further, that commitment is not undertaken simply by virtue of my intending to undertake it
findings.note: a speaker-level criterion that could be applied to a human–LLM pipeline as a whole

findings.position: Uttering words, even a performative formula, is not sufficient for a speech act. The entry's somniloquist case treats an utterance-producing system without speaker meaning as a non-speaker. This parallels 'parts as such do not speak'.
findings.who: Green (the entry)
findings.quote: while talking in my sleep I might say, "I hereby promise to climb the Eiffel Tower," without thereby making any promise
findings.note: a ready analogue for an LLM component emitting speech-act-shaped strings

findings.position: Non-human or non-standard speakers are not excluded in principle. Searle allows a dog requesting to be let out, and Davis's cases include speaking to photocopiers and infants. This sits against biological chauvinism, though neither point concerns speakers.
findings.who: Searle 1969; Davis 1992
findings.quote: Searle considers the case of a dog requesting to be let outside (1969, p. 39)
findings.note: the entry does not treat biology as the boundary; it just never asks about machines as speakers

findings.position: Millikan's biosemantic conventionalism grounds linguistic conventions in reproduced patterns and functions. A referee could use it to ask whether the stopping point lies in function or history. The entry also compares a speech act's characteristic aim to a biological trait's function.
findings.who: Millikan 1998 (the entry criticizes it)
findings.quote: the view that a speech act-type has a characteristic aim is akin to the view that a biological trait has a function
findings.note: the nearest biology-flavoured account of what grounds speech acts, and the entry finds it obscure

findings.position: Layered performance of acts: one speech act can be performed by performing another, and a further act can be performed through a set of intentionally performed acts. This is the entry's nearest analogue to 'authorship layered across levels'.
findings.who: Searle 1979, Bach & Harnish on indirect acts; Searle & Vanderveken on illocutionary commitment
findings.quote: she performs S n only by virtue of intentionally performing some other set of speech acts
findings.note: layering is among acts of one agent, not across components of a composite agent

findings.position: Attribution fixed by an institutional rule. Austin and Searle's force conventionalism and the preparatory conditions of authority and uptake make who performs an act depend on social rules. This is close to a 'separate attribution rule'.
findings.who: Austin 1962; Searle 1969; Searle & Vanderveken 1985; Langton on uptake
findings.quote: Only an appropriate authority, speaking at the appropriate time and place, can: christen a ship, pronounce a couple married
findings.note: a referee would ask whether the attribution rule is conventional (Austin/Searle) or intentional (Strawson/Green)

findings.position: Davidson's point that nothing in the utterance guarantees force, since actors and jokers can simulate it. A referee could use it to say that surface speech-act output from an LLM cannot settle authorship.
findings.who: Davidson 1979
findings.quote: every joker, storyteller, and actor will immediately take advantage of the strengthened mood to simulate assertion
findings.note: supports looking beyond the output to the intentions of the producing system

nearest_positions: Intentionalism about force (speech acts constituted by overt communicative intention) — Strawson 1964, Grice 1957, Green's overtness/commitment account
Force conventionalism (institutional rules fix who performs which act) — Austin 1962, Searle 1969
Biosemantic/natural-convention account of speech acts — Millikan 1998 (the entry criticizes it)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry never mentions LLMs or any machine as a candidate speaker or author. It does not mention Gubelmann or a Kantian criterion for agency or speakerhood. It says nothing on composite or collective speakers, on whole/part or organ relations, on layered authorship across levels, on a separate attribution rule for authorship, or on 'a third kind of author'. AI appears only in the opening list of fields influenced by speech act theory, plus Shoham 1993 in the bibliography with no discussion. All of the thesis's central apparatus is outside the entry.

theses: Gubelmann's Kantian criterion has no principled stopping point at the skin without biological chauvinism. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines, it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting whole, so 'LLMs cannot speak' reduces to 'parts as such do not speak'. The whole may be a speaker, with authorship layered across levels and fixed by a separate attribution rule. A distinct third kind of author is not established.
